title: Bodhidharma
hookLine: the legendary Indian monk Chan remembers at its beginning, sitting with his face to a wall

lines: A DOLL THAT ROCKS BACK UP.
cards: A blank wall. Rough plaster, a crack running down one corner. In front of it, a monk sits with his back to the room.
Visitors come and go behind him. He doesn't turn around. In paintings he's drawn with a thick beard, heavy brows and wide, unblinking eyes.

In Japan he became a round red doll with no arms or legs, weighted at the bottom, so every time you knock it over it rocks back upright. This is Bodhidharma, the monk Chan remembers at its beginning in China.

teach.h: A MONK FROM INDIA, MOSTLY LEGEND.
teach.b: First, who he was, as far as anyone can say. Tradition says he was a monk from India, some accounts say from the south and from a royal family, who came to China to teach.

Beyond that, little about him is certain, and the stories grew longer and more colorful in the retelling. So it's honest to call him legendary: a real memory, wrapped in a great deal of story. Second, facing the wall.
The Chan stories say he settled at a monastery on Mount Song and sat facing a wall, for years, saying little.
A short teaching attributed to him speaks of wall-gazing: settling the mind so it stands like a wall, unmoved, with no difference left between self and other.

Whether the wall was a real wall, a picture of the mind, or both, the image stuck. Third, the first ancestor. Chan tells its history as a line of teachers handing the teaching to students, mind to mind.
In that line, Bodhidharma is counted as the first ancestor in China, the link back to India. The next few days bring the emperor who didn't understand him and the student who did. Fourth, why a wall.
A wall gives you nothing: no view, no story, nothing to scroll.
What's left is whatever the mind brings. That's the point. The red doll in Japan carries the same idea in a lighter key: knocked over, it comes back up, the way attention comes back after it wanders.

how: In Soto Zen meditation halls in Japan, practitioners sit facing the wall, and Chan and Zen temples honor Bodhidharma's image as the first ancestor.

games.q: you're a monk newly arrived in a far country, with a teaching that's hard to put into words. what do you do?
o: write a long book explaining everything.
go to a mountain monastery and sit facing a wall.
travel from town to town giving lectures.
games.why: the Chan stories say Bodhidharma settled on Mount Song and sat facing a wall, saying little. the wall became the teaching.

practice: If you can, turn toward a plain wall, close enough to see it but not so close you strain, and let your eyes rest half open on one spot; if you can't, lower your gaze to the floor.
When a thought appears, let it play against the wall like a shadow, and pass. When you notice you've drifted, come back, like the doll rocking upright.

wordCard.voice: Bodhidharma. The legendary monk from India whom Chan counts as its first ancestor in China, remembered sitting with his face to a wall.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Bodhidharma, the name of the monk; bodhi is awakening, dharma the teaching.

carryVoice: Your line: facing the wall. Nothing to look at, and the mind shows up anyway. Day nine hundred eleven, done.
